claims.text: Adding a uniform nanoscale dispersion of Y2O3 to a tungsten-based refractory high-entropy alloy will improve its radiation tolerance.
The Y2O3-modified alloy will maintain mechanical integrity under fusion-reactor plasma-facing conditions.
Mechanical alloying followed by spark plasma sintering at 1200–1300 °C can produce a uniform dispersion of Y2O3 nanoparticles in the alloy.
A uniform nanoscale Y2O3 dispersion will remain stable at oxide/matrix interfaces in the alloy.
Y2O3 particles will create a high density of oxide/matrix interfaces.
The oxide/matrix interfaces will act as sinks for radiation-induced vacancies and interstitials.
Defect absorption at the oxide/matrix interfaces will suppress the formation and growth of radiation-induced defect clusters.
Defect absorption at the oxide/matrix interfaces will suppress void formation and growth.
The Y2O3-modified alloy will have lower irradiation-induced defect density than the unmodified alloy.
The Y2O3-modified alloy will exhibit less irradiation-induced void swelling than the unmodified alloy.
The Y2O3-modified alloy will maintain or slightly improve high-temperature mechanical properties relative to the unmodified alloy.
An unmodified powder-metallurgy tungsten-based refractory high-entropy alloy typically accumulates more defects and undergoes more swelling during irradiation than its Y2O3-modified counterpart.
The proposed benefits depend on achieving a uniform nanoscale Y2O3 dispersion.
A nonuniform dispersoid distribution could reduce defect-sink efficacy and mechanical benefits.
The proposed effect is expected to hold during irradiation at 400–600 °C.
Extended irradiation may destabilize the Y2O3 dispersoids.
A nonuniform Y2O3 dispersion may cause local embrittlement.
